segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had finished giving instructions to his twelve disciples, he moved on from there to teach and proclaim in their towns.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now when John heard in prison about the works of the Messiah, he sent word through his disciples

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect someone else?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go and report to John what you hear and see:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: the blind see again and the lame walk, those with skin disease are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised and the poor are brought good news.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then what did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way before you.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet the least in the kingdom of the heavens is greater than he.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of the heavens has been suffering violence, and the violent are seizing it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah, who is to come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has ears hear.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces who call out to the others

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and say, ‘We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her works.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he began to reproach the towns in which most of his deeds of power had been done, because they had not turned back:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? You will go down to Hades. For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to infants.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yes, Father, for this was what pleased you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Come to me, all you who toil and are burdened, and I will give you rest.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

notes.note: The Greek has the article (“the Christ”) and uses the word as a title for the anointed king Israel expected, not as a name. “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. “Christ” is kept where the word works as part of Jesus’ name.

The Greek word names people with the scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which made a person ritually unclean; this is why they are “cleansed” and not simply healed. “Leper” today means someone with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the biblical term and may not be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers” with a footnote; the conditions involved were serious and brought social exclusion.

notes.phrase: the poor are brought good news
notes.traditional: the poor have the gospel preached to them
notes.note: Jesus’ answer is a chain of phrases from Isaiah’s pictures of God’s coming restoration (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1; compare 26:19). He does not answer John’s question directly but points to what is happening and leaves John to draw the conclusion. The verb is the ordinary Greek word for announcing good news, traditionally rendered “preach the gospel.”

notes.traditional: be offended in me; take offense at me
notes.note: The verb comes from a word for a trap or obstacle and means to be tripped up in one’s trust or loyalty. “Offended” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Modern versions are divided here between “takes no offense at me” and “does not stumble on account of me.”
The quotation follows Malachi 3:1, with wording that also recalls Exodus 23:20. The Greek word for “messenger” is the same one usually rendered “angel”; here it refers to a human herald.

Matthew’s characteristic phrase has “heavens” in the plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The meaning is the same as “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels.

The Greek verb can be read as passive (“suffers violence”) or as middle (“advances forcefully”), and this is one of the most disputed sayings in the Gospels. The passive is taken here, with “the violent” understood as hostile, which fits John’s imprisonment. Others read the saying positively, of eager people pressing into the kingdom (compare Luke 16:16).

notes.phrase: he is Elijah, who is to come
notes.note: Malachi 4:5 (3:23 in the Hebrew numbering) promises that Elijah will be sent before the day of the Lord, and many expected his return ahead of God’s decisive intervention. Jesus identifies John as the one who fills that role.

The verb belongs to the word-family that English divides between “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify.” Here it means to be shown to be in the right, which “vindicated” says more plainly than “justified.” Many modern translations render it the same way.

Many manuscripts read “children” in place of “works,” matching the parallel in Luke 7:35. “Works” has early support and is preferred by most editors, since copyists would more likely have altered Matthew to match Luke than the reverse. It also ties back to “the works of the Messiah” in verse 2.

The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural for acts that display it. There is no dispute about the meaning; “miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering. “Deeds of power” is chosen so that the link with the word “power” elsewhere stays visible.

“Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

notes.phrase: You will go down to Hades
notes.note: The taunt echoes Isaiah 14:13–15, addressed to the king of Babylon, who aimed to ascend to heaven and was brought down to the realm of the dead. Hades here is that realm, the lowest place as heaven is the highest, and is distinct from the place of final punishment. Some manuscripts read “you will be brought down.”
“Meek” now suggests weakness, which the Greek word does not; it describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentle” or “humble” is the mainstream modern rendering.
A yoke was a familiar Jewish image for submitting to instruction, used of wisdom’s teaching (as in Sirach 51:26) and of the Law. “You will find rest for your souls” echoes Jeremiah 6:16.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament and versions split between “preach” and “proclaim,” which carry different modern connotations.
“This generation” is a recurring and theologically weighty phrase in the Gospels, and translators sometimes vary it with “age” or “kind of people.”
The word covers everything from Galilean villages to Jerusalem and Rome, and an unprincipled alternation between “city” and “town” would confuse readers.
The verb means “confess” (sins) in some places and “praise, thank, acknowledge” in others, and versions divide between “thank” and “praise” here and in the Luke parallel.
Versions vary between “wilderness,” “desert” and “deserted place,” and the word carries Exodus and Isaiah associations that consistent English would preserve.
